parole.significato: only used in 'sto qua and 'sto qui
parole.testo: Clipping of esto, from Latin istum, accusative masculine singular of iste (“that”, pronoun), of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare questo, codesto and stesso.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the present participle of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -antem.

parole.significato: added to a verb or adjective to form a masculine abstract noun
parole.testo: From Latin -ōrem, for earlier -ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *-ōs, for original **-oss.

parole.significato: raw thread, reduced to skeins, of linen, hemp, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin acia, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).

Inherited from Late Latin aciārium, derived from Latin aciēs (“sharp point”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Cognates include French acier, Friulian açâr, Galician aceiro, Portuguese aço, Romansh atschal, and Spanish acero.
Borrowed from Latin acuēre, from acuō (“to sharpen”).
From earlier aco, from Latin acus (“needle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). Compare Romanian ac.
From earlier *acucchia, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”), Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-. Doublet of aguglia, which was borrowed from Occitan.
From Latin algentem, present active participle of algeō (“to be, feel cold”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *h₂elgʰ- (“frost, cold”).
From Latin algōrem (“cold”), from the verb algeō (“to be, feel cold”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *h₂elgʰ- (“frost, cold”).
From alto (“high, tall”) + -iero; alto is from Latin altus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow; to nourish”).
Learned borrowing from Latin altōrem (“nourisher”), derived from alō (“to foster, nourish”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”).
Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

From alveolo (“alveolus”) + -are (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin alveolus (“small cavity”), derived from alveus (“hollow, cavity”), from alvus (“belly, womb”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”).
From Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).
Borrowed from Latin angulus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng-, *ang- (“corner, hirn”).
Borrowed from Latin anguem, form of anguis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngʷʰis (“snake”).

From Latin angustus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰ-. The correspondence of Latin short /u/ to Italian /u/ (rather than Italian /o/ as in agosto, mosto) indicates that the form is possibly a semi-learned borrowing (compare gusto).
From Latin ante, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“opposite, in front of”).
From Latin arātrum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
Borrowed from Latin arietem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r-i-(e)t- (“certain domestic animal”).
From Classical Latin hariolus, derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰerH- (“bowels, intestines”).
From Latin artem (“art”, “skill”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tís, from the root *h₂er- (“to join, put together”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin articulus, derived from artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tús. Compare also the doublet artiglio.
From Latin asperum (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese áspero (“rough”), French âpre, Romanian aspru.
Inherited from Latin axis, axem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”).
From Latin avus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os. Compare Portuguese avô (“grandfather”) and avó (“grandmother”).
Borrowed from Latin baculum, from Proto-Indo-European *bakklom, derived from the root *bak- (“stick”). Doublet of bacchio.
Inherited from Late Latin ballāre.
Borrowed from Latin blandus.
Inherited from Latin kalendae.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *canālia, from canis, corresponding to cane + -aglia.
From Latin carbōnem (“charcoal; coal”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”).

parole.significato: common hornbeam, European hornbeam (tree, Carpinus betulus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin carpinus, probably from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂er- (“hard”).
From Latin cavum, cavus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”).
From Latin cicer, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱiḱer- (“pea”).
Learned borrowing from Latin celer, celerem.
From Latin cella, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelnā.
From Latin cinerem, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”).
Probably an early borrowing from Latin cerebrum (“brain, skull”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂s- (“head”). Cf. the related cervello, which was inherited from a diminutive of the Latin word.
Inherited from Latin cervīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head”) and *weyk- (“to bend”), borrowed in modern senses.
From Latin cervus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂wós, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).
From Latin quid (but also usurping some roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.
From Latin quod, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod.
From Latin quis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos.
From Latin clāmāre, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”). Doublet of clamare, a borrowing.
From Latin cicōnia, derived from Proto-Indo-European *kekoh₂n-, from the root *keh₂n- (“to sing”).
From Latin cilium, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel-yo-m, which is derived from *ḱel- (“to cover”).
Derived from Latin citāre (“to summon”), from cieō (“move, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-.
Inherited from Late Latin collīna, from the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”) + -ina, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”).
From Latin collum, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolsom, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to turn”). Cognate with French cou, Galician and Portuguese colo, Sicilian coḍḍu, Spanish cuello.
From Latin colōrem, from Old Latin colos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).
From Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of verb colō (“to till, to cultivate”), originating from Proto-Indo-European *kʷl̥tós, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to turn”). Doublet of culto.
From Latin cuneus, whence also cuneo (a borrowed doublet). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱū (“sting”).

parole.significato: body (the physical structure of a human or animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowing corpus.
From Latin curtus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Derived from Late Latin creātūra, from Latin creō.
Inherited from Latin crispus, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Borrowed from Latin cribrum, from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to sieve”). Compare the inherited old Italian crivo, and related crivello.
Inherited from Latin crusta, from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).

From Latin cultus (“reverence, adoration, veneration”), noun use of the perfect passive participle of colō (“to cultivate; to worship”), originating from Proto-Indo-European *kʷl̥tós, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to turn”). Doublet of colto.
From Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“to cultivate; to inhabit”), originating from Proto-Indo-European *kʷl̥tós.
From Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
Derived from Latin curvus (“bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).

parole.significato: one who guards or keeps watch:
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin custōdem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, hide”).
Borrowed from Latin dēnsus.

parole.significato: bright, resplendent, shining (in a divine fashion)
parole.testo: From Latin dīus, alternative form of dīvus (“divine, godlike”), from Proto-Indo-European *diwyós (“heavenly”), derived from the root *dyew- (“sky, heaven”).
Inherited from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. See also s-.
From Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”).
From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”), from dē + Latin māne, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).
From Latin hedera, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to seize, grasp, take”).
From Latin illum (“that”), from earlier olle, from Old Latin ollus (“he, that”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“beyond, other”).
From Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).
Latinizing modification of state, inherited from Latin aestātem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“burn; fire”).

parole.significato: scythe (larger tool than sickle); sickle (smaller tool than scythe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin falcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelk-, *dʰelg- (“a cutting tool”). Compare French faux.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *falciāre (compare French faucher), from Latin falx (“sickle, scythe”), from Proto-Indo-European *dhalk-, *dhalg- (“a cutting tool”).
Borrowed from Latin fāma, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-mā-, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).
Inherited from Latin famem (“hunger”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Portuguese fome and Romanian foame, Sicilian fami.
Inherited from Latin faba, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”).
From Latin favus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).
Inherited from Latin febrem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰris, an extension of the root *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn, warm”).
From Latin fidem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-.

parole.significato: to wound, to injure, to hurt
parole.testo: From Latin ferīre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.
From Vulgar Latin *fervere, from Classical Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to be hot, boil”).
From Latin fissus (“split, cloven”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidtós (“id”).
Derived from Latin fibra.

From Latin faenum (“hay”), which derives from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-. Another proposed etymology is a Vulgar Latin *flēnum, from a blending of flōs (“flower”) and faenum. Cognate with Sicilian frenu.

Inherited from Latin fīlia, from fīlius (“child, son”), from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fille, Portuguese filha, Galician filla, Romanian fie, Spanish hija, Sicilian figghia, Sardini

From Latin fīlius, from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fils, Portuguese filho, Galician fillo, Romanian fiu, Spanish hijo, Sicilian figghiu, Corsican figliu, Sardinian fillu, Romansh feg

parole.significato: to pretend; to feign; to dissemble
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fingere (“to fashion, make up”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”).
From Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium (“leaf”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

parole.significato: source, spring (where a body of water emerges)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fontem m, of Proto-Indo-European origin.
From Latin formīca, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *morwi. Cognates include Ancient Greek μύρμηξ (múrmēx).
From Latin futuere (“to fuck”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”).

parole.significato: to have a strong pleasant smell or fragrance
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fragrāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreHg- (“to smell, to have a strong odor”).

parole.significato: common ash, European ash, ash (tree, Fraxinus excelsior)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fraxinus, from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”).

Inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, found in a Pompeian inscription), itself from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos. Doublet of
Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
Borrowed from Latin frīgidus, from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sriges-, *sriHges-. Compare the inherited doublet freddo.
From Latin fūstis (with the addition of an onomatopoeic r), possibly from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʷʰen- (“to slay, kill”).
From Latin fūlīginem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-.

From Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo (“frost, cold”) + -ato (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.” Akin to Russian моро́женое (moróženoje).
Borrowed from Latin gelidus, derived from gelū, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *gel- (“cold”).
From Latin gelū (“frost, chill”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).
From Latin generum, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.
From Latin gingīva, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
Borrowed from Latin genius.

parole.significato: gens (legally defined unit of Roman society)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tim. Doublet of genesi via Ancient Greek, and compare etymology 1.
From Latin glāns, glāndem, with change in declension, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂- (“acorn”). Compare French gland, Romanian ghindă.
From Latin glomus (“ball”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“form into a ball; ball”).
From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

From Latin diurnālis (with influence from giorno (“day”)), from Latin diurnus, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Originally an adjective meaning "daily" (modern giornaliero) as a modifier for foglio giornale.
From Latin iuvencus (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós, derived from *h₂yuh₁en-, derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force”, “life”).
From Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”).
From Vulgar Latin *graclu(s), syncopated form of Latin grāculus (“jackdaw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare English grackle, Spanish grajo, and Portuguese gralho.
From Latin grandinem (“hail”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₃d-.
Past participle of granire (“to granulate”), from grano (“grain”), from Latin granum (“grain”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain”).
Inherited from Latin grānum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
From Latin gruem f or m (“crane”), from Proto-Indo-European *gr̥h₂ú-, from *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”). Cognate with French grue f, Spanish grua f, Portuguese grou m, Romanian grui m.
From Latin grumus, from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).
A Dantean Latinism borrowed from Latin ignem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis (“fire”).

parole.significato: not to know, to ignore, to be unaware of
parole.testo: From Latin īgnōrāre.

parole.significato: located in the lowest or innermost part
parole.testo: From Latin īmus, superlative form of īnferus (“low”, “deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
From Latin in-, a prefixation of in (“in, into”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.

parole.significato: used to denote negation or opposition or privation; un-; in-; a-
parole.testo: From Latin in- (“un-, not”), from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, zero grade form of the sentence negative *né.
From Latin īnferiōrem, comparative form of īnferus (“low, deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
From Latin īnferus (“low”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
From Latin īnfimus, superlative form of īnferus (“low, deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
From Latin īnsomnis, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From Latin īnsomnia, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
Inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).
Inherited from Latin labrum, related to labium, from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang down”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of the lips”), derived from Latin labium (“lip”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”).

From labiale (“labial”) + -izzare, from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of the lips”), derived from Latin labium (“lip”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”). By surface analysis, labial(e) (“labial”) + -izzare (“-ize”, verbal derivational suffix).
Inherited from Old Italian laco, from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).

parole.significato: period (of time). only used in lasso di tempo (“period of time”).
parole.testo: From Latin lāpsus, perfect participle of lābor (“to slip, flow”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
From Latin lātus (“wide”, “broad”), from earlier stlātus, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to stretch out, extend, spread”) or *stelh₃- (“broad”).
From Latin lavāre (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).
From Latin līma (“a file”).
From Latin līmus (“mud, slime”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”).
From Latin līnum, from Proto-Indo-European *līnom.
From Latin laudem, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lēwt-, *lēwdʰ- (“song, sound”), from *lēw- (“to sound, resound, sing out”).
Inherited from Latin luctārī.

From Latin lūcus (“grove sacred to a deity”), from Old Latin loucos, from Proto-Indo-European *lowkós (“open space, clearing”), derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include English lea (“meadow”), Hindi लोक (lok, “public” ← “world”), Lithuanian laũkas (“field”).

Learned borrowing from Classical Latin lūcubrāre (“to work at night or by candlelight or lamplight”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-o-dʰro-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”).
From Latin longus (“long, extended”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).
Inherited from Latin mancus, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂n-ko- (“maimed in the hand”), from *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én- (“hand”).

parole.significato: margin, border, edge, brink, bank, brow
parole.testo: From Latin marginem, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs.
Inherited from Latin mātūrus, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).

parole.significato: member (one who belongs to a group; an element of a set)
parole.testo: From Latin membrum (“member; limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *memso-, *mems-ro (“flesh”).
From Latin mentem, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”).
From Latin mentum, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”).

parole.significato: to put, to place, to lay, to set
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French mettre, Spanish meter, Occitan metre, and English mission.
From Latin metere, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to mow, reap”).
Inherited from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Inherited from Latin meliōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”).
From Vulgar Latin *mucceus, from Latin mūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slimy, slippery”).
From Latin modus, from Proto-Indo-European *modós, derived from the root *med- (“to measure”).
Inherited from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).

parole.significato: much, very much, a lot (with verbs)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.
Inherited from Latin mortem, from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).
From Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-. Compare Spanish mosca.
From Latin mustum, neuter of mustus (“fresh, young", and, of wine, "unfermented”), from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”). Cognate with Sicilian mustu.
Inherited from Latin mūgīre, from Proto-Indo-European *mug-, *mūg-, of onomatopoeic origin.
From Vulgar Latin mungere, from Classical Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ-.
From Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).

From Latin mūscus, probably through a diminutive Vulgar Latin root *mūsclus, from syncopation of an earlier *mūsculus. Compare Romanian mușchi, Friulian muscli. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.
Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

From Latin nebula, through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nebla. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Sicilian negghia, Venetan nebia, Spanish niebla, Romanian negură and Aromanian negurã. Doublet of nebula, which was borrowed.
Learned borrowing from Latin naevus, from earlier gnaevus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁iwós (“native”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget”). Doublet of neo.
Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).
From Late Latin nonna.
Inherited from Late Latin nonnus.
From Latin nocturnus, from noctū (“by night”), from nox (“night”), whence also Italian notte, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.
Inherited from Latin numerus (via old intermediary forms *nomero > *nombero > *nobero), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). Doublet of numero, a borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.
From Vulgar Latin oclus, syncopated from Latin oculus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Doublet of oculo, a borrowing.
From Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
From Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.
From Latin humerus, umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”).
From Latin unda, from nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
Borrowed from Latin onus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃énh₂os, from the root *h₃enh₂- (“to onerate, charge”).
From Latin onustus (“burdened”, “loaded”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃enh₂ostos, from the root *h₃enh₂- (“to onerate, charge”).

Inherited from Latin orbus (“orphaned, deprived”) (probably a clipping of the phrase orbus ab oculīs (“deprived of eyes”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Compare Sicilian orbu, Romanian orb, and French aveugle from a different clipping of the phrase.
From Latin ornus, from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-.
From Latin hortus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰortós.
From Latin hordeum (see there for cognates), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”). Compare Sicilian oriu.
From Latin uter, from earlier *udris, from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water”).
From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
From Latin pācem (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.
Inherited from Latin palea, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
From Latin palātum.
From Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂.
Inherited from Latin pānem, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”).
From Latin parāre, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).
From Latin passer remodeled as a third-declension noun, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”).
From Latin picem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pī́ts (“pitch; resin”).
Borrowed from Latin pecūlium (“property, savings”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *peḱu- (“livestock, domestic animals”).
From Latin peiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”).
Inherited from Latin pellis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).
From Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-.
From Latin pānis.

parole.significato: to strike, to hit, to beat
parole.testo: From Latin percutere (“to strike, beat”), from per- + quatiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₁t- (“to shake”). Cognate with English percuss, French percuter.
Inherited from Latin piscem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.
Inherited from Latin plangō, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-. Compare Spanish plañir, Catalan plànyer, Romanian plânge, French plaindre.

Uncertain. Possibly from: * An onomatopoeic root or children's/nursery word *pikk-, *picc-. * From Vulgar Latin *pikk (“little”), related to *piccāre (“to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”). * From picca (“point”). * From Vulgar Latin pittitus (“small, wo
From Late Latin peduclus, contracted form of peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, diminutive of pēdis (“louse”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-. Compare Sicilian pidicchiu.
From Latin pedem (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. Compare Catalan peu, French pied, Piedmontese pé, Latvian pēda, Lithuanian pėdės, Portuguese pé, Sardinian pei, Spanish pie.
From earlier *piecare, from Latin plicāre, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”).

parole.significato: pine, pine tree (tree of the genus Pinus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”).

Inherited from Latin plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, *pelh₁u- (“many”). The initial autogemination, though lost in standard pronunciation, is still found in most varieties of regional Italian. The gemination occurs predictably before the palatalization of the original
From Latin pluri-, combining form of plūris, from plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“many”). Related to plenty, plural (via Latin) and fele, full (via PIE).
From Late Latin pullastra, from Latin pullus (“chick, chicken”) + -aster, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”). Compare Sicilian puddastra.
Masculine form of pollastra from Late Latin pullastra, from Latin pullus (“chick, chicken”) + -aster, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”). Compare Sicilian puddastra.
From Latin pullus, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”).
From Latin pulmōnem, from Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō.
From Latin pulpa, from Old Latin *pelpa, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Unrelated to polpo (“octopus”).
Inherited from Latin pulverem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”). Doublet of polve, from the Latin nominative pulvis. Akin to Sicilian prùvula.

parole.significato: the ridge between two furrows; balk
parole.testo: From Latin porca (“balk”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥ḱeh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“to dig”).
Inherited from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).
Inherited from Latin portāre (“to bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).

parole.significato: well (hole sunk into the ground as a source of water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin puteus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *paw- (“to strike”).
Inherited from Latin prandium, whence also Dalmatian prinz and Romanian prânz. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin.
From Latin praeda, from earlier praeheda, from prae- + Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to hold”).

parole.significato: to take, hold, pick up, get
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendere (“take, seize”) (not attested without a prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
From Latin pugna, from pugnō (“to fight, oppose”), from pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
From Latin pūlicem, from Proto-Indo-European *plus- (“flea”).
From pupo, from Latin pūpus, from the Proto-Indo-European root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). By surface analysis, pup(o) (“puppet”) + -azzo (derivational suffix).
Inherited from Latin pūpus (“boy, child”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few; little”).
From Vulgar Latin *pūtīre, from a change in conjugation of Latin pūteō (“to stink”), derived from a form *pūtos, from Proto-Indo-European *puHtós, derived from the root *puH- (“rotten, foul”).
From Latin quadrātus, from quadrō (“to make square”), from quattuor (“four”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
From Late Latin quarranta, from Latin quadrāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”).
Inherited from Latin regīna.

From Italian reperto (“find, exhibit, report”), from Latin repertum (“discovery, finding again”), from Latin reperiō (“find, find out, learn, realize, discover, invent”), from re- + pario (“to give birth, bear, give birth to, beget”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forth”).
From Latin rēctus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós (“straightened, right”).
From Latin ēricius (“a hedgehog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”).

parole.significato: to ask for, demand, apply for
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *requaerere, from Latin requīrere with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/, from re- with quaerere, from Proto-Indo-European.
Inherited from Latin rīpa, from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to tear, cut”). Doublet of riva.

Borrowed from Latin rōbustus (“hard, solid”, literally “oaken, of oak”), derived from rōbur (“hard oak; hardness”), from ruber (“red”) (for its reddish hardwood), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Doublet of rubesto.
Inherited from Latin rōdere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”).
From Latin rogāre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-, Indo-European ablaut of *h₃reǵ-.
From Latin rōbur (“hard oak”, “hardness”), from ruber (“red”) (for its reddish hardwood), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Cognate with Sicilian rùvulu.
From Latin ērūca, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer(s)-uk-eh₂, from *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”). Doublet of eruca.
Inherited from Latin ruga, from Proto-Indo-European *krewp- (“to become encrusted”), extension of *krew- (“scab”).

parole.significato: willow (tree of the genus Salix; the wood of this tree)
parole.testo: From Latin salix, from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”). Doublet of Salgari.
From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).
From Late Latin sanguem, alteration of Classical Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare French sang, Romanian sânge.
From Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scelus, from Proto-Indo-European *skélos, derived from the root *(s)kel- (“bent, crooked”). Cognate with Greek σκέλος (skélos, “leg”).
From earlier *scuto, from Latin scūtum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), an extension of *sek- (“to cut”).
Inherited from Latin secūrem.
From secco, from Latin siccus, from a Proto-Indo-European root *seyk-. By surface analysis, secco (“dry”) + -ezza (“-ness”, nominal derivational suffix).
From Latin siccus, from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.
From Latin signum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”) or *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
Variant of sevo, from Latin sēbum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”). Cf. also sebo.
From Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
From Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”).
Inherited from Latin sēmen, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.
From Latin sēmi-, from Proto-Indo-European *sēmi (“half”).

Attested from ca. 1261. A cross of inherited sempice, semprice with Latin simplicem, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”) + *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare duplice, molteplice. Partial doublet of scempio.
Borrowed from Latin senem, from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).
From Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).
Inherited from Latin serpentem, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.

parole.significato: servile (of or pertaining to a slave)
parole.testo: From Latin servus, from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.
From Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).
From Latin sitim, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“decay; destruction”), derived from the root *dʰgʷʰey- (“to decline; to perish”).
From Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).
From earlier segnore, from Latin seniōrem, comparative form of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos. Doublet of sire.
From Latin situs (“laid, placed”), perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”), from Proto-Indo-European *si-n-H-, n-infix of the root *sey(H)- (“to put”).
From Latin socius, from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare the doublet socio.

parole.significato: member, affiliate, partner, associate, fellow, mate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷyo- (“companion”), derived from the root *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare also the inherited soccio.
From Latin solium (“seat, throne”), from Proto-Indo-European *sodyom, derived from *sed- (“to sit”).
From Latin sulcus, from Proto-Indo-European *solk-o- (“furrow”), *selk- (“to pull, drag”).
From Sole, from Latin sōlem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥. Cognates include Greek ήλιος (ílios), Icelandic sól, Hindi सूर्य (sūrya), and Russian со́лнце (sólnce).
From Latin somnolentus, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From Late Latin somnolentia, derived from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
Learned borrowing from Latin sopīre.

From Latin sopōriferum, derived from sopor (“sleep”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *swep- (“to sleep”). By surface analysis, sopor(e) (“sleep”) + -ifero (“bearing”, “carrying”, adjectival derivational suffix).
From Latin surdus (“silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).
From Latin spargere (“to scatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).
Inherited from Latin spīrāre (“to breathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys-.
From Latin spurcus, with vowel shift reinforced by contamination of porco, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.
From Latin sporta.
Borrowed from Latin stimulus.

parole.significato: to clasp, to grasp, to grab tightly, to hold tightly
parole.testo: From Latin stringere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūculare, *succulare, from sūcus (“juice, sap, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *suk-. Compare Latin sūgō (“suck”) (< Proto-Indo-European *sug⁽ʰ⁾-), Italian sucare.
Inherited from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.
Inherited from Latin sūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-. Cognate to English succulent via Latin. Doublet of succo. Cognate with Sicilian sucu.
From Latin socerus, variant of socer, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros.
From Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).
Inherited from Latin tenerum, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
Inherited from Latin terminus or the variant termen, termine, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”).

Learned borrowing from Latin testis, from earlier *terstis ← *tristis, from Proto-Indo-European *tristh₂s (“a third party standing, after the two parties to a contract or dispute”), from *tréyes (“three”) and *steh₂- (“to stand”).
Inherited from Latin tingere (“to dye, to paint”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to soak, to dip”).
From Latin turdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.
From Latin torvus.
From Latin trāns (“across, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of tras- and trans-.
Inherited from Latin trīgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).
From Latin tonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). By surface analysis, tuono + -are.

From ubriaco (“drunk”) + -are, from Late Latin ēbriācus, derived from Latin ēbrius, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”). By surface analysis, ubriac(o) (“drunk”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).
From Late Latin ēbriācus, derived from Latin ēbrius, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”). Cognate with Sicilian mmriacu.
From Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”).

From earlier officio, borrowed from Latin officium (“duty, office”), derived from ops (“wealth, resources”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₃ep- (“to work”). Doublet of opificio and officina.
From Latin ūndecim.
Dissimilation of inherited Latin ululāre (“to howl”), ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.
Inherited from Latin vacca.
From Vulgar Latin *valliāre, from Latin vallus, from Proto-Indo-European *wal- (“stick, stake”).
From vagliare, from Vulgar Latin *valliāre, from Latin vallus, from Proto-Indo-European *wal- (“stick, stake”).
From Latin vicis.
From Latin vēlum, from Proto-Indo-European.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.
From Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.
From Latin venereus, venerius (“of or relating to sexual love”), from Venus (“Roman goddess of love”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”)) + -eus, -ius.
From Latin ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.
From Latin virga (“twig, stick”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgeh₂ (“flexible rod or stick”).
Derived from Latin vice.
Inherited from Latin vīcus, from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”).
Learned borrowing from Latin virum (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós.
Borrowed from Late Latin vīrulentus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wisós (“poison; slime; fluidity”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, from earlier volva, from the Proto-Indo-European root *welH- (“to turn, wind”).
